title: Barbera
description: Piedmont's most planted red: deep colour, bright acidity, low tannin and a natural love of food.
L: Barbera gives deep ruby wines with sour and black cherry, plum, raspberry and dried herbs. Its signature is high acidity with low tannin, an unusual balance for a dark grape. That makes it juicy and refreshing. It's Piedmont's most planted red grape.

Barbera's skins are rich in colour pigments but low in tannin. Its acidity stays high even when fully ripe, partly due to high levels of malic acid. In the 1980s, producers like Giacomo Bologna began ageing it in small new oak barrels; oak adds the tannin Barbera lacks and softens its acidity.
Why did producers begin ageing Barbera in new oak?
To add the tannin it naturally lacks
Oak adds structure and tannin, balancing Barbera's high acidity.

Look for deep ruby colour, cherry fruit, a mouth-watering acidity and very little grip from tannin. Oaked versions add vanilla and spice. It's darker than Nebbiolo but much softer in tannin, and more acidic than Dolcetto.
Barbera is known for very high tannin.
Not true. Barbera is low in tannin; its acidity is what stands out.
Barbera gives cherry fruit with high acidity and low tannin
Oak, since the 1980s, adds the tannin it lacks

Barbera's two main zones are Asti and Alba. Barbera d'Asti, a DOCG since 2008, is the larger zone, often lighter and fresher, with Nizza, a DOCG since 2014, as its top area. Barbera d'Alba, a DOC, grows on sites not given to Nebbiolo, giving fuller, richer wines.
Barbera d'Asti and Nizza; Barbera d'Alba

Barbera grows in Lombardy's Oltrepò Pavese and Emilia-Romagna, where it's sometimes made fizzy. Italian immigrants took it to California and Argentina. Australia has small plantings. Its high acidity makes it useful in hot climates, where it keeps freshness.
Match each zone to its Barbera.
Each zone gives Barbera a different weight.
Nizza is Barbera's top tier: a minimum of 18 months' ageing, 6 in wood, and grapes from the hills around Nizza Monferrato.
Why is Barbera useful in hot climates?
Its natural acidity keeps wines fresh even in heat.
Barbera d'Asti and Nizza are DOCGs; Barbera d'Alba is richer
It also grows in Lombardy, Emilia, California and Argentina
Its acidity is useful in warm regions

Barbera's high acidity and low tannin make it one of the most food-friendly reds. It suits tomato sauces, pizza, lasagne, salumi, fatty meats and even mushrooms. It cuts through richness without clashing. In Piedmont, it goes with bagna cauda, a warm garlic and anchovy dip.

Serve at 15 to 17 degrees. Unoaked Barbera is best within three years. Oaked Barbera d'Alba, d'Asti Superiore and Nizza can age five to ten years. Its acidity helps it keep, but fruit fades before structure develops.
Unoaked young; oaked five to ten years
Why does Barbera suit tomato-based dishes?
Its high acidity matches tomato's acidity

Good Barbera balances its acidity with ripe fruit. Overcropped Barbera tastes thin and sour. Lower yields, older vines and good sites give more depth. In the 1980s, producers' new focus turned it from a peasant wine into a respected one.
Sweet desserts make dry red taste sour.
Barbera's acidity makes it very food-friendly
Unoaked is best young; oaked lasts five to ten years
That balance makes it juicy and food-friendly.
Barbera's story is one of transformation.
What does new oak bring to Barbera?
Barbera is Piedmont's most ____ red grape.
It covers more of Piedmont than Nebbiolo or Dolcetto.
Barbera has high acidity and low tannin
Asti, Nizza and Alba are its key zones
It's one of the most food-friendly reds
